modules.module: M1: Why Hardware Determines AI Capability

Claude.notes: Narrative scenes (Edison/bulb, AlexNet 2012, Jensen Huang 2006, Oct 7 2022, ChatGPT at scale) effectively set up the concept sections that follow, but the module lacks a recurring protagonist who lands the insight — history is reported to the learner rather than discovered by a character. Narrative density is below the 20–35% Advanced target; most of each lesson is exposition. Quizzes and the Module Test lean heavily on recall of dates, numbers, and names rather than requiring the learner to apply the hardware-forecasting mental model the lessons promise.
Claude.topIssue: No protagonist arc — insights are delivered as expository claims rather than earned through a character's reasoning, and the four lessons do not share a connective story thread.

Gemini.notes: Technical scaffolding is generally solid: FLOP, CUDA, Tensor Cores, HBM, EUV, and the fabless model are defined accurately. A few precision slips: the FLOP key-term says 'arithmetic calculation on a decimal number' when the correct phrasing is 'floating-point number'; the Tensor Core description 'performs 64 multiplications per clock cycle' conflates per-core FMA throughput with the 4×4×4 matrix-multiply-accumulate primitive Volta actually executes; and 'cache-miss latency' is attributed to GPUs in ways that gloss over the real latency sources in GPU inference (warp scheduling, HBM round-trip). Labs are discussion-only chat exercises that never require the learner to run a benchmark, inspect a hardware spec sheet, or reason over real data — a significant weakness for a technical-depth course at the Advanced tier.
Gemini.topIssue: FLOP definition says 'decimal number' instead of 'floating-point number' — a minor but concrete technical inaccuracy inside a key-term card that learners will read as authoritative.

Perplexity.notes: Content is anchored to the 2022–2024 landscape and feels noticeably dated for a late-2026 learner. The flagship NVIDIA chips discussed are A100 (2020) and H100 (2022), with no mention of Blackwell (B100/B200, 2024), GB200/NVL72, or the Rubin generation now in flight. AMD stops at MI300X (2023) — no MI325X or MI350. Google TPU coverage stops at v4; Trillium (v6, 2024) and Ironwood are absent. The 'export controls' section covers October 2022 and October 2023 rules but misses the December 2024 and January 2025 updates, Huawei's Ascend 910C, and the DeepSeek-V3 moment that reframed compute-efficiency arguments. Groq's LLaMA 2 demo (early 2024) is 2+ years old; today's live comparisons would use LLaMA 3.3/4 or DeepSeek on Groq, Cerebras, and SambaNova. Scaling-laws framing also does not acknowledge the post-DeepSeek re-examination of efficient-training versus raw-compute theses. The labs reference 2025 decisions ('advising a mid-size AI company in 2025'), making the whole hardware narrative read as a snapshot the learner has to mentally fast-forward.
Perplexity.topIssue: The module treats H100/A100 as the current frontier and omits Blackwell, Rubin, Trillium, MI325X/MI350, and the December 2024 / January 2025 export-control updates — the hardware landscape has moved an entire generation past what this lesson describes.

Claude.notes: Advanced-tier module with four lesson vignettes (CUDA 2006, Volta 2017, Market 2023-24, Challengers from Google 2016) that each tee up the concept well. Story density is on the light side for an Advanced lesson — vignettes are single paragraphs that feel like garnish on heavy concept blocks rather than a threaded narrative. Gold-callouts routinely hand the learner the punchline ('Strategic Lens', 'Key Insight') instead of letting them derive it. Delivery is clean: consistent lesson hero → sections → callouts → quiz → lab rhythm, clear tab navigation, well-structured timelines and stat grids. The biggest curriculum weakness is D5: the labs are all variants of the same chat-with-an-assistant pattern, and 14 of 15 module-test questions are recall rather than judgment.
Claude.topIssue: Quiz and module-test questions are mostly year/number/product recall; only one of 15 forces applied judgment (Q15 on challenger strategy).

Gemini.notes: Technically the content is solid for an Advanced tier audience. Definitions of CUDA, cuDNN, kernel, Tensor Core, systolic array, Transformer Engine, BF16/FP8, and NVLink are all directionally correct. Two technical imprecisions worth noting: (1) the description of Tensor Cores as computing 'D = A×B + C in a single clock cycle for small matrix tiles' overstates what the MMA instruction actually does — the operation is pipelined and the stated throughput is per-core-per-cycle rather than per matrix MMA — a learner could reasonably come away misunderstanding the latency vs throughput picture. (2) Meta's Llama 3 cluster figure of ~49,000 H100s conflates the two-24K-cluster architecture Meta published with a rounded aggregate; the paper itself reports per-run GPU counts closer to 16K. H100 list-price range ($30K–$40K wholesale / $40K+ with SXM / $60K spot) is reasonable. The 3,958 TFLOPS FP8 spec, 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s bandwidth, and 900 GB/s NVLink 4.0 figures match NVIDIA's published numbers.
Gemini.topIssue: Tensor Core description ('compute D=A×B+C in a single clock cycle') overstates per-instruction latency and could mislead on throughput vs latency trade-offs.

Perplexity.notes: Historical facts (CUDA 2006, AlexNet 2012, cuDNN 2014, Volta 2017, Ampere 2020, Hopper 2022) are durable. The currency problem: this module's 'present tense' is frozen in 2023-early 2024. NVIDIA data center revenue is anchored at FY2024's $47.5B, but by 2026 NVIDIA has reported multiple subsequent fiscal years with substantially higher data-center revenue — the headline stat and its framing ('up from $15B the prior year') are stale and understate current concentration. The Blackwell GB200 NVL72 section treats the product as cutting-edge new; by late 2026 Blackwell is shipping and Rubin-generation announcements would be the frontier. 'As of 2024, neither [AMD ROCm nor Intel oneAPI] has closed the ecosystem gap' is still broadly true but needs a 2025-2026 update on ROCm 6/7 maturity and the Trainium 2/3 and Maia 100 generation progression that have happened since. TSMC node references (4nm H100, 3nm/2nm roadmap) are accurate as-written but miss the N3E / N2 rollout that is now part of the live narrative. Labs work (Claude API is still available in 2026) but the prompts read as a 2024 snapshot.
Perplexity.topIssue: Headline market data (NVIDIA FY2024 data-center revenue, Blackwell as cutting-edge, ROCm/Trainium framed 'as of 2024') is two years out of date relative to a 2026 reader.

Claude.notes: Narrative is sparse but appropriate for Advanced-tier density (~20%). The 2013 projection story in L1 creates a crisp problem that the rest of the lesson answers, but the three later lessons (L2–L4) lean almost entirely on exposition with only brief story-scene framings. Named characters (Jeff Dean, Sundar Pichai, Thomas Kurian) appear as anchors but never develop — they sign off decisions and vanish. Concept depth and 'why' framing are excellent; the module reliably asks strategic rather than factual questions. Lab executability is the softest point: four AI-tutor chat labs that work but keep the learner in a passive Socratic exchange rather than driving any applied analysis.
Claude.topIssue: Learner is told, not shown — the insight structure across L2–L4 is largely expository, with story-scenes used as scene-setters rather than as a path the learner walks toward the concept.

Gemini.notes: Technical fidelity is strong throughout. TPU v1 specs (256×256 systolic array, 8-bit integer MACs, 92 TOPS at 40W, 28 MB on-chip SRAM, 256 GB/s to DRAM, PCIe) are all accurate; the Jouppi et al. 2017 figure of 15–30× perf/W on Google's six production workloads vs Haswell Xeon and K80 is cited correctly along with its precision/workload caveats. bfloat16 is defined correctly (8-bit exponent matching float32, 7 mantissa bits, trading precision for dynamic range), HBM bandwidth figures for v2 (600 GB/s) and v3 (900 GB/s) match disclosure, and the TPU v4 optical circuit switching / 4,096-chip pod / ~1 exaFLOP description aligns with the June 2023 Nature paper's claims. Crucially, the module actively prevents the common misconception that TPUs 'beat' NVIDIA, and that the 2017 15–30× advantage still applies — both are addressed head-on in L3.
Gemini.topIssue: Minor imprecision in L3 where the H100's NVLink Switch System is described as giving '900 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth per GPU' — NVLink 4 per-GPU bandwidth is 900 GB/s aggregate (450 GB/s each direction); the phrasing could mislead a technical reader into misreading the direction split.

Perplexity.notes: Historically accurate through roughly May 2024, which is also the 'current' edge of the content. The core TPU v1→v6 arc, Axion's April 2024 announcement, and Trillium at I/O 2024 are all correctly represented. However, from a late-2026 vantage this reads as dated: TPU v7 'Ironwood' (announced April 2025) is used as a fake distractor in mt13, which is now a confusing anachronism; NVIDIA's Blackwell (B100/B200) and H200 generations — now the dominant frontier training chips — are absent; MLPerf 4.x/5.x results superseding the v3.1 Nov-2023 comparison are not acknowledged; and Trillium is described as 'available in Google's own infrastructure... with Cloud TPU availability to follow' when it has been Cloud-GA for well over a year. The strategic takeaways (independence, ecosystem lock-in, JAX/XLA risk) hold up, but a learner using this today will leave with a 2024-era mental model of the hardware race.
Perplexity.topIssue: mt13 distractors treat 'Ironwood' and 'Pathways Chip' as fictional, but Ironwood (TPU v7) was publicly announced in April 2025 — the quiz item will now actively confuse a learner who has followed the field since.

Claude.notes: Strong Advanced-tier concept scaffolding across the hyperscaler + startup silicon landscape, with sharp cognitive framing (vertical integration, memory-bandwidth-bound inference, latency vs throughput moats). Narrative under-indexes — each lesson opens with a short 'Context' scene then becomes dense exposition, so protagonists never discover anything themselves; the labs invite reflection but the lesson body never dramatizes a decision. Also, registry metadata says M4 = 'The New Entrants' with subtitle 'AMD, Intel, Cerebras, Groq' but the actual lessons cover Google/AWS/Microsoft plus the four startups — the module overshoots its registry subtitle.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative density is well below the Advanced 20–35% target: story-scenes are brief lead-ins only; the body is told, not discovered, so the 'learner lands the insight' criterion is weakly met.

Gemini.notes: Technical scaffolding is credible but some specifications are compressed in ways a close reader could challenge. The 'TPU v1 delivered 10× perf/watt vs GPU' phrasing in L1 conflates two different numbers from the ISCA 2017 paper: ~15–30× speedup versus K80/Haswell, and ~30–80× energy efficiency — the module later cites 15–30× perf/watt in the Module Test, which is also a compression. 'Jonathan Ross first proposed the TPU' is a simplification — Ross was one of the originators and the key hardware lead, but the proposal is usually attributed to a small team including Norm Jouppi. The Trillium '4.7× compute performance per chip over TPU v5e' claim reflects Google's peak-compute marketing figure, not sustained workload performance. The 'Inferentia 16nm TSMC' spec is correct. NeuronLink, EFA, systolic array, wafer-scale, RDU, tensor streaming processor definitions are all accurate.
Gemini.topIssue: The TPU v1 perf/watt number conflates speedup and energy-efficiency figures from the ISCA 2017 paper — a learner reading this will cite '15–30× perf/watt' as if that is the paper's single headline figure.

Perplexity.notes: Freshness is the weak link. The module's silicon landscape stops at mid-2024 (Trillium/TPU v6, Trainium2 UltraClusters, Maia 100, Groq Series D). Reading this in late 2026, a learner would get no mention of NVIDIA Blackwell B200 shipping in volume through 2025, the Blackwell Ultra / Rubin cadence, AWS Trainium3 previewed at re:Invent 2024, Microsoft Maia 2, the Cerebras IPO trajectory, Groq's expanded partnerships, Google Axion Arm CPU, or the Apple–Broadcom / Meta MTIA v2 silicon tracks that widened the 'new entrants' field. The core concepts (systolic arrays, memory-bandwidth-bound inference, latency vs throughput) remain correct and durable, but the specific examples and benchmarks feel 12–18 months stale.
Perplexity.topIssue: The module is anchored to 2023–mid-2024 silicon releases; by late 2026 the Blackwell generation, Trainium3, Maia 2, and the Meta/Apple in-house silicon programs are missing, so the 'current competitive landscape' framing is outdated.

Claude.notes: Story-scene anchors (Transformer 2017, Fiji 2015, FlashAttention 2022, the fundamental distance-vs-capacitance problem) bind each lesson's concept to a concrete inflection point, and the concept-to-concept flow — bandwidth fundamentals → HBM → attention bandwidth → beyond-HBM — reads as a purposeful curriculum arc rather than a grab-bag of topics. Delivery architecture is strong: clear kicker labels, consistent lesson→quiz→lab tiles, and a module-test gate keyed to lesson/quiz completion. Where the narrative thins is c2 Learner Insight — the story scenes present history as told rather than letting the learner discover the bandwidth-wall insight themselves — and c3 Density, which sits at the lean end of what an Advanced-tier narrative can carry.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative tells the historical insight rather than staging it so the learner arrives at the bandwidth-wall conclusion themselves.

Gemini.notes: Core technical definitions are precise and appropriately deep for Advanced: arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte), the Roofline ridge point, through-silicon vias, silicon interposers, HBM generational specs, O(N²) attention memory complexity, FlashAttention tiling, grouped-query attention, PIM, UCIe, UALink, and co-packaged optics all land accurately. Hardware figures check out (H100 HBM3 ~3.35 TB/s, V100 HBM2 900 GB/s, Fiji R9 Fury X 512 GB/s, Wulf–McKee 54%/7% growth gap). Misconception-prevention work is strong — the module actively flags that HBM's advantage is width not speed, that FlashAttention is exact not approximate, that attention is bandwidth- not compute-bound. The factual soft spot is the real-world case anchor in L3 and MT10: the KV-cache sample calculation attributes 64 KV heads to Llama 2 70B, but Llama 2 70B uses GQA with 8 KV heads, putting its real KV cache at ~2.5 GB/4K context rather than ~20 GB. The module's own Q11 later correctly describes Llama 2 70B as a GQA model, creating an internal inconsistency a technical reviewer immediately catches.
Gemini.topIssue: L3/MT10 compute Llama 2 70B's KV cache as if it used 64 KV heads; Llama 2 70B uses GQA with 8 KV heads, so the headline ~20 GB figure is ~8× too large for that specific model.

Perplexity.notes: Content is well-sourced for 2022–2024 but is clearly vintage mid-2024 rather than late-2026. The flagship accelerators throughout are H100 and H200 with HBM3/HBM3e; by November 2026 a current-landscape module would be built around NVIDIA Blackwell (B100/B200, GB200 NVL72), HBM4 in volume on SK Hynix/Micron/Samsung, and early Rubin-generation disclosures — none of which appear. The L4 outlook still frames HBM4 as 'targeting 2025–2026' as if it were future-tense, when it is now the current generation. The 2023 HBM supply crunch is described in the past tense correctly, but the module does not surface the 2025 Samsung HBM3e qualification turnaround or the ongoing HBM4 allocation dynamics that would matter to a current learner. The lab's hardcoded model string `claude-opus-4-5` is also stale (current is Opus 4.7 / 5.5), which would surface as a 404-class error on today's proxy. Labs are executable thanks to the offline-fallback mode, and the capability-delta framing is clean.
Perplexity.topIssue: Hardware landscape is anchored to H100/H200 and treats HBM4 as forthcoming; a 2026 reader needs Blackwell B200/GB200 NVL72 and in-production HBM4 as the reference frame.

Claude.notes: Story vignettes (Microsoft/Azure ChatGPT scale-up, Jensen's Hopper launch, Groq LPU launch, OpenAI's $700K/day bill) effectively set up each lesson's technical tension, but they function as brief framing devices rather than sustained narrative arcs; no recurring protagonist or cast carries through. The concept sections tell more than they let the learner derive — e.g., the roofline model is introduced and explained rather than discovered through a calculation the learner performs. Narrative density is well-calibrated for Advanced tier (~20-25% story), and the story→concept→quiz→lab rhythm is consistent across all four lessons. The capability delta is primarily analytical: the learner can explain splits, not build them.
Claude.topIssue: Chatbot-based labs let the learner converse about hardware tradeoffs but never produce a concrete artifact (a roofline calculation, a cost model, an annotated architecture diagram), weakening the applied-outcome delta despite strong conceptual framing.

Gemini.notes: Technical foundations are largely correct: arithmetic intensity, KV cache mechanics, roofline model, systolic arrays, FSDP sharding proportionality, PagedAttention's role in fragmentation reduction, and tensor-parallel all-reduce frequency are accurately described. Numerical claims are mostly in the right range: A100 312 TFLOPS BF16, H100 ~989 TFLOPS BF16 on SXM, Llama 2 70B ~1.72M A100-hours, and the A100 memory-bandwidth figures all match public references. However, the H100 NVL is cited at '188 GB of HBM3e' — the standard H100 NVL ships with 94 GB HBM3 per card (188 GB is the paired-card SKU total, which the text does not clarify) and 'HBM3e' is strictly an H200/B100 feature. The 'near-FP16 accuracy with roughly 2× throughput' claim for the Transformer Engine's FP8 path mirrors NVIDIA marketing language without noting that FP8 training stability still varies across model families and layer types. The INT4 'quarter-bandwidth' line glosses over the fact that INT4 weight-only quantization typically needs calibration or GPTQ-style methods to preserve accuracy.
Gemini.topIssue: The H100 NVL '188 GB of HBM3e' line conflates single-card capacity with paired-card SKU totals and misstates the memory generation — an Advanced-tier module is the one place that spec precision matters most.

Perplexity.notes: Real-world case selection is reasonable for a 2023/2024 snapshot — Groq LPU public launch (Feb 2024), the OpenAI/Azure ~$700K/day reporting (late 2023), Meta's Llama 2 disclosures, the Anthropic–AWS $4B partnership, and SemiAnalysis's 'inference exceeds training spend by 2025' projection are all credibly sourced. The gap is currency: by late 2026 the hardware landscape has moved on substantially, and the module reads as if frozen in early 2024. NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B100 and FP4 are mentioned only as a one-sentence roadmap note; H200 (141 GB HBM3e), GB200 NVL72, and real production Trainium2/TPU v5p/v6e deployments are absent. Groq's 300 tok/s figure for Llama 2 70B is period-correct but newer public benchmarks on Llama 3.1/3.3 70B would strengthen the claim. The 'by 2025' SemiAnalysis estimate is now testable and could be reframed as a confirmed/refuted prediction rather than a forecast. Lab 3's chip menu (Groq LPU · Inferentia2 · TPU v5e · L40S) omits the chips an engineer would actually benchmark today (H200, GB200, Trainium2).
Perplexity.topIssue: The lab menu and chip comparisons are frozen at early-2024 options — a learner following this today would evaluate a stale slate that excludes H200, Blackwell, Trainium2, and current-generation Groq/Cerebras cloud offerings.

Claude.notes: Strong Advanced-tier module. Context vignettes (May 2019 Huawei, Oct 7 2022, Jan 2025 DeepSeek) are compact but effectively set up each lesson's problem. Concept architecture is coherent: definitions → case detail → gold-callout limits. Lab system prompts are specific, grounded, and give the AI tutor real substantive material to engage with. Module Test is well-sequenced from framework → cases → strategic assessment. Narrative is deliberately thin — appropriate for the Advanced register, but relies on exposition rather than learner-discovered insight.
Claude.topIssue: Story-scene vignettes read as exposition rather than scenes where the learner arrives at an insight; the 'problem that the concept answers' is stated rather than discovered.

Gemini.notes: Technical substance is largely accurate and impressively specific: Big Fund phases and amounts, YMTC 232-layer NAND, SMIC Dec 2020 Entity List, FDP Rule mechanics, CHIPS Act $52.7B, DeepSeek R1 ~2,048 H800 cluster. The October 2022 Nvidia-threshold explanation blurs two distinct BIS metrics — aggregate chip-to-chip interconnect bandwidth (originally expressed in GB/s) and 'bandwidth density' (Gbps/mm²). The module uses '600 Gbps/mm²' as a single parameter in multiple places (L2 text, Q2-2, MT-7) in a way that conflates these. The 4,800 TOPS INT8 figure is a reasonable rounded approximation for 'TPP × bit length' but readers may misread it as a raw INT8 TOPS cap.
Gemini.topIssue: The 600 Gbps/mm² interconnect-density figure conflates BIS's chip-to-chip bidirectional bandwidth threshold (originally GB/s) with a separately introduced performance-density metric — a technical imprecision repeated in both lesson text and module test.

Perplexity.notes: Through January 2025 (DeepSeek R1, Biden AI Diffusion Framework) the content is accurate and current. For a learner reading this in late 2026, however, the storyline freezes at the handoff moment. The Trump administration's early-2025 reversal and reissuance of the AI Diffusion Rule, subsequent 2025 BIS actions on Huawei Ascend 910C/920, the SMIC N+2 yield debate, the H20 secondary-market restrictions, and post-DeepSeek R1 Chinese model releases (V3, R2-class) are all absent. The L4 'DeepSeek Moment' gold-callout frames the issue well but would land harder if updated to 2025–2026 context. Lab prompts still function because they reference enduring frameworks (EAR, FDP, Wassenaar) rather than specific month-level news.
Perplexity.topIssue: Content ends at January 2025 and does not mention the Trump administration's revision of the AI Diffusion Framework, post-DeepSeek R1 Chinese model developments, or 2025–2026 Huawei Ascend / SMIC advances — material a 2026 learner will expect in a module on this topic.

Claude.notes: Each lesson opens with a crisp dated 'Context' scene (NVIDIA FY24 revenue, Google TPU 2016 disclosure, Loihi 2 Sept 2021, Oct 7 2022 BIS rules) that genuinely sets up the concept problem that follows. The 'Pivot Point' and 'Pattern' callouts carry the insight work, though they often tell rather than let the learner arrive at them. Narrative density sits around 15-20% of each lesson — on the thin side for even an Advanced tier but defensible given the density of technical scaffolding. There are no recurring characters, which is appropriate for a systems-level module. Story→concept→quiz→lab→next-lesson flow is consistent and well-tabbed. The weak seam is D5: the labs are AI-chat discussion prompts rather than hands-on exercises (a roofline plotter, TCO calculator, or systolic-array visualizer would have fit the subject), and the quizzes lean heavily on recall of specific figures (watts, transistor counts, token/sec, year of deployment) rather than judgment. The capability delta ('explain the post-GPU landscape and its geopolitics') is real but understand-level, not do-level.
Claude.topIssue: Labs are chat-based discussion prompts for a hardware module that cries out for an interactive artifact — a roofline/arithmetic-intensity visualizer or a cost/power calculator — so the applied-outcome dimension underperforms.

Gemini.notes: Core technical definitions are largely correct at an advanced register: SIMD, HBM, roofline model, systolic array, Kirchhoff's current law + Ohm's law as the basis of analog MAC, memristor, EUV lithography, CUDA moat — all consistent with primary literature. Real cases are cited with dates and sources (Google's 2017 ISCA TPU paper, IBM's 2023 Nature Electronics PCM inference result, Cerebras WSE-3 March 2024 launch, Groq Llama-2 70B >300 tok/s Dec 2023, Huawei Ascend 910B on SMIC 7nm). Misconception avoidance is strong: the module explicitly says analog is inference-only (device drift limits to ~4-bit), photonic needs DAC/ADC boundaries, and none of the alternatives threatens GPU training today. Two technical imprecisions keep c1 off a 4: the Loihi 2 energy figure quoted as '~1 mW per million synaptic operations per second' implies ~1 nJ per synaptic operation, which is roughly an order of magnitude higher than the per-SOP energies Intel reports (~pJ-range); and the ResNet-50 ImageNet accuracy '92.81% top-1' attributed to IBM's 2023 PCM analog chip conflates different mixed-signal demonstrations in the literature — the figure is directionally correct but the one-sentence attribution understates the mixed-precision digital assist involved. These are precision issues, not conceptual errors.
Gemini.topIssue: Loihi 2 is characterized as '~1 mW per million synaptic operations per second,' which implies ~1 nJ/SOP — off by roughly an order of magnitude from the per-SOP energies Intel publishes; the sentence should either re-express efficiency in pJ/SOP or qualify the operating regime.

Perplexity.notes: The content is anchored almost entirely to Q1 2024 datapoints (NVIDIA FY24 Q4 earnings, March 2024 WSE-3 launch, Meta early-2024 MI300X Llama milestone, Oct 2023 export-control tightening). For a module living in a Nov 2026 curriculum, that's ~2.5 years of unreferenced evolution. Missing currency flags: the Blackwell (B200/GB200) transition in early 2025 has made several H100-based comparisons outdated (700W TDP and 3.35 TB/s are now one generation behind); Groq's production inference scale-up and Aramco/Saudi deployments (late 2024) would modernize the LPU story; IBM NorthPole (2023/2024) deserves explicit mention alongside the PCM analog work since it's now the canonical IBM AI inference chip the press references; Lightmatter's 2024 >$400M round and the Passage photonic interconnect production ramp would refresh the photonic section; Rain AI and Tenstorrent get no mention at all; the TSMC Arizona fab reached its first 4nm volume milestone in 2024-2025, which the module notes but doesn't update. Real-world cases cited are accurate but dated — hence c2 drops to 3. The labs still run (any current AI assistant answers these prompts), but the 'capability delta' a learner leaves with is a 2024 map of the hardware race, not a 2026 one; that's why D5 c3 lands at 3.
Perplexity.topIssue: The module's entire frame of reference is Q1 2024 — no Blackwell transition, no IBM NorthPole, no Groq production scale-up at Aramco, no Lightmatter 2024 funding, no mention of Rain AI or Tenstorrent; for a Nov 2026 curriculum this is one full generation behind.
